section_1.title: Prerequisite Visualization: The Circle vs. The Sphere
section_1.content: Establish foundational knowledge: A sphere is a 3D object defined by a constant radius 'r' from a center point. Contrast this with a 2D circle. Introduce the concept of a 'parallel light source' (orthogonal projection) to set the stage for shadows.
section_1.example: Animation: A 2D circle spinning into a 3D sphere, highlighting that the sphere's 'shadow' at any angle is always a perfect circle.

section_2.title: The Geometry of the Shadow
section_2.content: Explain that when light rays are parallel, the shadow of a sphere is a cross-section of the sphere passing through its center. Mathematically, the area of this shadow is equal to the area of a circle with the same radius: A_shadow = πr².
section_2.example: Visual: An astronaut on a moon base holds a spherical orb; the shadow cast on the lunar surface is shown to be a circle with radius 'r', regardless of which way the orb is tilted.

section_3.title: Sphere Surface Area: The Archimedes Insight
section_3.content: Introduce the formula for the surface area of a sphere: S = 4πr². Use a comparative logic: The surface area of a sphere is exactly four times the area of its projected shadow (the 'great circle').
section_3.example: Animation: Four circular 'shadow discs' are shown being 'unrolled' or wrapped around a sphere like a peel, perfectly covering its surface.

section_4.title: Synthesis and Practical Application
section_4.content: Synthesize the relationship: Area_surface = 4 × Area_shadow. Discuss why this is critical in fields like thermodynamics (heat radiation) or solar energy capture, where surface area determines absorption capacity.
section_4.example: Device: A spherical solar collector robot. The robot calculates its total surface area (for heat dissipation) as 4 times the area of the shadow it casts on the ground (its energy-capturing cross-section).

section_5.title: Summary and Quick Quiz
section_5.content: Review the core ratio 4:1. Encourage students to visualize the sphere not just as a volume, but as an object defined by its relationship to light and planes.
section_5.example: Quick visual test: If a spherical ball casts a shadow with an area of 10cm², what is the ball's total surface area? (Answer: 40cm²).
